How the tax bill is figured

Your property's assessed market value is the starting number. A state rate converts it to taxable value, and the local levy turns that into general tax by multiplying taxable value by mills and dividing by 1,000. One mill means $1 of tax on each $1,000 of taxable value. Your appraisal notice lists last year's total mills set by the taxing bodies where you live.

General tax is not always the whole bill. Charges for solid waste, street lighting and special or rural improvement districts can ride along, and the county treasurer will explain any line you do not recognize.

A higher value on your notice does not mean a matching jump in tax, since rates and levies move as well. The 2025 to 2026 appraisal cycle values property as of January 1, 2024. The previous cycle covered 2023 to 2024, with a January 1, 2022 value date. Expect the bill in late October. A seller should open it right away, because its due dates shape the closing.

Due dates and penalties

MCA 15-16-102 splits the year's tax into two payments. November 30 at 5 p.m. is the first deadline, extended to 30 days after postmark if the notice went out late. May 31 at 5 p.m. is the second. If either lands on a Saturday or holiday, you have until 5 p.m. the next business day, free of penalty and interest.

Tax left unpaid turns delinquent. Interest of 5/6 of 1% builds each month it stays open, and a flat 2% penalty is added. Paying the current year without the delinquent years is allowed. Money aimed at delinquent taxes, though, is credited to the oldest year first.

Owners of a primary residence can spread the bill out. Seven equal payments, each one-seventh of the total, fall on these dates: November 30, December 31, January 31, February 28, March 31, April 30 and May 31. Miss one and the normal interest and penalty apply.

  • Read the bill ahead of closing so the title company can quote an exact payoff.
  • Ask the treasurer whether special assessments are included.
  • Find out if the house is enrolled for a reduced rate rather than assuming the standard one.

2026 Montana property tax rates

Use decides the rate. For 2026, a qualifying owner-occupied home or long-term rental is taxed on a sliding scale that opens at 0.76%. A second home, short-term rental or vacant residential lot is charged one flat 1.90%.

Property use, 2026Rate
Home you live in, or a long-term rental: first $378,0000.76%
Same home, next slice up to $756,0000.90%
Same home, $756,001 through $1,511,9991.10%
Same home, value beyond that1.90%
Second home, short-term rental, empty lot1.90%
Apartment-style long-term rentals1.10%
Commercial or industrial, below $2,274,0001.50%
Commercial or industrial, $2,274,000 and up1.90%
Agricultural land that does not qualify14.35%
Agricultural land that qualifies2.05%
Forest land0.37%

Farm and forest parcels with a house are split. The house and its one-acre homesite get the sliding residential scale when the owner lives there or rents it long term. If the house is a second home or short-term rental, the rate is 1.90% on non-qualified agricultural and forest parcels and 1.35% on qualified agricultural ones. A parcel of 160 or more acres counts as agricultural on its own, and a smaller one has to show agricultural use and income.

Homestead exemption and other relief

Two reduced rates carry most of the relief. The Homestead Reduced Rate covers the owner's own principal residence. The Long-Term Rental Reduced Rate covers a home leased out in stays of 28 days or more for at least seven months. Enrollment goes through the Department of Revenue. The window for 2027 opened May 4, 2026 and closes March 1, 2027, and the department matches enrollment to the property geocode.

A lien notice from the county treasurer has to list the help on offer under MCA 15-17-125: the homestead reduced tax rate, the rental property reduced tax rate, state property tax assistance, and the residential property tax credit for the elderly.

Eligibility, enrollment and what happens when you sell are laid out in our Montana homestead exemption guide. Struggling with a bill? Raise these programs with the treasurer or the Department of Revenue early, ahead of any lien.

Tax liens: when they attach

Real property taxes that remain delinquent lead to a lien, attached by the county treasurer by the first working day in August at the latest. Proper notice is a condition. The county keeps the lien unless it assigns it to a third party, and where notice was defective no lien may attach (MCA 15-17-125).

A mailed warning has to go out two weeks or more before attachment. Once the lien is on, the treasurer signs a tax lien certificate, files a copy with the clerk and recorder, and mails another to the person assessed.

  • The certificate gives the delinquency date and the date the lien attached.
  • Tax, penalties, interest and costs are itemized separately.
  • It cautions that a tax deed may follow and states the date the county or an assignee can claim one.

Counties post their own cutoff dates inside that framework, so phone your treasurer for this year's lien date. The tax deed step comes later, with a notice window of May 1 to May 30 in the redemption year. A sale that closes before the lien attaches keeps the payoff simple.

Selling with taxes owed

Get a current payoff from the county treasurer and let the closing statement settle it. Delinquent bills, lien certificates and even a running tax deed clock do not stop a sale. The balance is paid from the proceeds, and the title company requires that.

Timing matters here. The title company works from the treasurer's payoff figure, so a bill that is current on the closing day usually makes for a clean, quick settlement, while a delinquent one adds interest and penalty until the payoff clears. Before fixing a closing date:

  • Check the appraisal notice for the classification and value the Department of Revenue assigned.
  • See whether the reduced rate is active, since it ends at year end after a sale.
  • Ask the treasurer about earlier-year delinquency, penalties and interest.
  • If the value looks wrong, use the review deadline printed on the notice.

Behind on taxes? Cash Home Buyers can make an as-is cash offer, and since the title company pays the balance out of the proceeds at closing, you need not raise the money first. Nothing here is legal or tax advice. Exact figures come from the county treasurer or the Department of Revenue.

Frequently asked questions

When are property taxes due in Montana?

The first half is due November 30 (5 p.m.), or 30 days after the notice postmark if that is later. The second half is due May 31 (5 p.m.). Bills usually arrive in late October.

What is the penalty for late Montana property tax?

Interest of 5/6 of 1% per month runs on delinquent tax until it is paid, and a 2% penalty is added on top (MCA 15-16-102).

Can I pay Montana property tax monthly?

Yes, for a primary residence. Seven installments are due on the last day of each month from November 30 through May 31, and a missed one brings interest and penalty.

What is the Montana property tax rate on a second home in 2026?

1.90% flat. Short-term rentals and vacant residential lots pay the same.

When does Montana attach a tax lien?

By the first working day in August, following a mailed notice at least two weeks earlier (MCA 15-17-125).

title: Montana Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home
content:
Montana Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home

Cash Home Buyers in Montana
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Montana Homestead Exemption: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Montana Homestead Exemption sale
  • Turn the Montana Homestead Exemption offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Montana House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Montana?
We buy Montana houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Two programs called homestead in Montana

Montana uses the word homestead for two separate programs, and sellers often mix them up. One lowers the property tax rate on a home you live in. The other protects home equity from creditors.

The tax program is the Homestead Reduced Rate. It applies to owners who occupy their Montana home as a principal residence for at least seven months per year, and it carries a lower rate than standard Class 4 residential property. The creditor protection is a homestead declaration, filed with the county clerk and recorder. A declaration does not qualify you for the reduced rate.

Which one matters depends on why you are selling. If the house carries a tax bill you cannot keep up with, the reduced rate is the tool. If a judgment creditor is circling, the declaration is the tool. Many owners need neither, but find out which one is already attached to the house before you list it or take an offer.

The reduced rate lowers property tax, is claimed through the Department of Revenue, and requires the home to be your principal residence for at least seven months a year. It is open to individuals, couples and revocable grantor trusts. The declaration protects equity from creditors, is recorded with the county clerk and recorder, and states that you reside on the premises.

Who qualifies for the Homestead Reduced Rate?

You qualify when the home is your principal residence for at least seven months a year, you or your revocable grantor trust own it, you are current on property taxes, and it is the only residence you claim the rate for.

The seven months do not have to run back to back. Short absences such as vacations, medical stays or military deployments generally do not cost you eligibility if the home remains your principal residence. Renting the house for a few months does not disqualify it either. The department's example is an owner who lives there from April through December and rents from January to March.

  • Properties owned by an LLC, partnership, corporation or irrevocable trust are not eligible for the homestead rate.
  • If there are several owners, the property qualifies as long as one owner meets the test.
  • Being behind on prior-year taxes disqualifies you. For 2026 taxes, current means paid in full or the first-half payment made.
  • You generally cannot claim the rate while also claiming a homestead in another state.

Homes owned through an LLC or irrevocable trust can still qualify for the separate Long-Term Rental Reduced Rate if they are rented to tenants for 28 or more days at a time, for at least seven months a year, as the tenant's residence.

2026 tax rates for a Montana homestead

For tax year 2026, a qualifying homestead is taxed in tiers. Each slice of value is taxed at its own rate, not the whole value at one rate.

Montana property tax rates by property type, 2026
Property typeTax rate
Homestead, first $378,0000.76%
Homestead, $378,001 to $756,0000.90%
Homestead, $756,001 to $1,511,9991.10%
Homestead, $1,512,000 and above1.90%
Second homes, short-term rentals, vacant residential lots1.90% flat
Multifamily used as long-term rentals1.10% flat

The gap between the homestead tiers and the 1.90% flat rate is why a sale in Montana can change the tax picture. A buyer who will not live in the house, or who plans to run it as a vacation rental, faces the higher flat rate. A buyer who will live there can enroll and expect the lower tiers. The Department of Revenue 2026 page lists the rates.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Montana house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to enroll and when

Enrollment goes through the Department of Revenue's Homestead.mt.gov pages, online or by mailed application. The application period for the 2027 tax year runs from May 4, 2026 to March 1, 2027.

You attest that the property meets the ownership, use, residency and tax-payment criteria. A false attestation can cost you the classification and bring legal and financial penalties.

Some owners do not need to enroll again. If you received the 2025 property tax rebate and still own and live in the same home, you are already enrolled. You must enroll if you moved, no longer use the home as your principal residence, the property was sold or transferred, or ownership changed since the rebate. New construction needs its own application.

  • Check enrollment with the Homestead Enrollment Verification Tool, using the property geocode.
  • Find the geocode through the Montana Cadastral site or property.mt.gov by searching the address or owner name.
  • Call the Department of Revenue Call Center at 406-444-6900 or visit a local field office for eligibility questions.

What happens to the reduced rate when you sell?

The reduced rate stays with the property through the end of the calendar year in which it sells, and the buyer must enroll to keep it going into the next year. The rate expires at year end, and buyers who will use the home as a principal residence need to enroll then.

If the house was not enrolled before the sale, the picture is different. A buyer who closes after the deadline on a home with no prior reduced-rate enrollment is taxed at a flat 1.9% for 2026. That buyer can claim a refund of the difference between the flat rate and the homestead rate between January 1 and May 31, 2027, after paying 2026 taxes in full and filing the refund form.

Timing also matters for people who sell one home and buy another in the same year. Months of residence can be combined if the two homes were occupied consecutively for seven months. If you sold in July and moved into the new house in August, the months count together. If the new home was not occupied until September, they do not.

For a seller, the practical points are short:

  • Confirm whether your house is enrolled before you quote a buyer anything about next year's taxes.
  • Pay every installment that is due so the house is not delinquent when the sale closes.
  • Tell the buyer to enroll as the new owner once the enrollment window is open.

How a Montana homestead declaration works

A declaration is a recorded document in which the owner states that they live on the property and claims it as a homestead. Under Montana Code Annotated 70-32-105, the person selecting a homestead must execute and acknowledge the declaration the same way a deed is acknowledged and file it for record. Section 70-32-106 requires a statement that the person is residing on the premises and claims them as a homestead, with a description of the premises. Section 70-32-107 requires recording in the county where the land sits.

The protection has a ceiling. Under 70-32-104, the homestead value limit was $350,000 in 2021 and rises 4% each calendar year after that. If you own an undivided interest, your exemption is proportional to your share. Section 70-32-201 makes the homestead exempt from execution or forced sale except as the chapter provides.

Sale proceeds get a limited shelter too. Under 70-32-213, money paid to the claimant from a sale, up to the exemption amount, keeps the same protection against legal process for 18 months. The Montana courts website offers a homestead declaration form and a form for declaring abandonment of a homestead, both on its estate planning and probate forms page.

If you are selling by choice, a declaration matters most when judgment liens or unpaid bills exist and you want to know how much of the proceeds you may keep. A Montana attorney can confirm how the limit applies to your facts.

Selling under tax or creditor pressure

Start by pulling the three facts that drive everything else: whether the house is enrolled for the reduced rate, whether property taxes are current, and whether a declaration was ever recorded.

  • Run the geocode through the enrollment verification tool to see the tax classification.
  • Ask the county treasurer for the current balance and any delinquent amounts, since delinquency also blocks the reduced rate.
  • Search the county clerk and recorder records for a homestead declaration and for judgment liens against the owner.
  • Look at your appraisal notice to see how the Department of Revenue classified the property.

Homes that are vacant, inherited, tenant-occupied or in disrepair often fall outside the reduced rate, so the 1.90% flat rate may already be in the tax bill. A cash buyer can price the house as it stands, and a title company clears recorded items at closing. This is general information, not legal or tax advice, so confirm details with the Department of Revenue or an attorney.

Frequently asked questions

Is the Montana homestead exemption the same as the homestead reduced tax rate?

No. The reduced tax rate lowers your property tax and is claimed through the Montana Department of Revenue. The homestead declaration protects home equity from creditors and is recorded with the county clerk and recorder. A declaration does not qualify you for the reduced rate.

How long do I have to live in the house to get the Montana homestead rate?

You must occupy it as your principal residence at least seven months each year. The months do not need to be consecutive, and short absences for vacations, medical stays or military deployments generally do not affect eligibility.

Does the homestead rate transfer to the buyer when I sell?

Only for the rest of that calendar year. The buyer must enroll as the new owner if they will live in the home. A home with no prior enrollment is taxed at a flat 1.9% for 2026, with a refund of the difference available January 1 to May 31, 2027 to a qualifying buyer.

How much equity does a Montana homestead declaration protect?

Under MCA 70-32-104 the limit was $350,000 in 2021 and increases 4% every calendar year after 2021. Co-owners of an undivided interest are limited to a proportional share. Confirm the current figure with a Montana attorney before relying on a specific number.

Who can I call with Montana homestead questions?

The Department of Revenue Call Center at 406-444-6900 handles eligibility questions, and the Homestead.mt.gov pages have the application and the enrollment verification tool.

title: Montana Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling
content:
Montana Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Montana Estate and Inheritance Tax sale

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Montana?
We buy Montana houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Does Montana have an estate or inheritance tax?

No. Montana no longer collects either one. The inheritance tax was repealed in November 2000 and does not apply to deaths after January 1, 2001, and the state has no estate tax for deaths after 2004.

For heirs, that means no Montana death tax return stands between a house and its sale. Montana also no longer requires a certificate or consent from the Department of Revenue to close probate or transfer securities. Other costs can still arise, and the sections below go through them.

Federal estate tax and a Montana house

Federal estate tax hits only large estates. A person who dies in 2026 has a $15,000,000 basic exclusion, and gifts made in 2026 are excluded up to $19,000 per recipient.

Death-tax rules that touch a Montana estate
Tax or exclusionAmount or rule
Montana inheritance taxRepealed; none for deaths after January 1, 2001
Montana estate taxNone for deaths after 2004
Federal basic exclusion, year of death 2026$15,000,000
Federal annual gift exclusion, 2026$19,000 per recipient

No federal estate tax is owed when the estate falls under the federal figure. A family that thinks the total might come close should talk to an estate attorney, because a house is only one asset in the count.

Taxes that can still apply when heirs sell

What remains is income tax on the estate, income tax on any gain, and property tax. These are not death taxes, yet each one can shrink what heirs take home.

  • Fiduciary income tax: the personal representative may need to file Montana Form FID-3 if a federal Form 1041 was filed and the decedent owned Montana property or had Montana-source income.
  • Capital gains: a sale for more than the basis produces a gain, covered in the next section.
  • Property tax: the county keeps billing the house, and the first half and second half dates keep running during probate.

Our Montana capital gains guide covers the income tax rates in detail.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Montana house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What is the tax basis of an inherited house?

Your basis in an inherited house is generally what it was worth on the day the owner died. Publication 551 treats that date-of-death value as the normal starting point for property that comes from a decedent.

When no Schedule A shows the estate tax value, the appraised value at the date of death can stand in for state inheritance or transmission tax purposes. Montana levies no such tax, so an independent appraisal is how most heirs document the number.

Spouses and joint owners follow special rules. When either spouse dies, the whole value of community property generally becomes the basis of the entire property. A surviving joint tenant or spouse who held title with the decedent should read Publication 551 closely.

Who can sell the house, and how probate affects that

Once appointed, the personal representative may sell estate real estate unless the will or a court order says otherwise. MCA 72-3-613, the state's probate code, covers a representative acting reasonably for the people with a stake in the estate. That person may dispose of land for cash or on credit, in a public or private sale.

Related powers include making repairs, leasing property, insuring assets, paying taxes and assessments, and hiring attorneys or agents. A limit written into the will, or an order from a formal proceeding, can narrow all of this, which is why buyers and title companies ask to see the letters of appointment.

Montana offers informal and formal probate, and the choice turns on the estate's size and whether a valid will exists. The courts' self-help page has a probate questionnaire, an affidavit of death, a small estate packet and a fiduciary statement.

Passing a house without probate

Some houses transfer on death without a court case, and the transfer is recorded with a form. The Montana Realty Transfer Certificate covers transfers by operation of law, including termination of a joint tenancy or life estate by death and a transfer on death deed. Attach the documents that match the transfer:

  • Joint tenancy or life estate ended by death: a certified death certificate.
  • Transfer on death deed: the recorded deed and a certified death certificate.
  • Court decree: a certified copy of the order or decree.

An optional form of transfer on death deed is available under MCA 72-6-415. Heirs who receive a house this way can sell it after recording, but they should have the title company review the chain of documents first.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Montana houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Property tax for an heir who does not live in the house

A person must actually live in the home to get the lower primary-residence rate. It starts at 0.76% on the first $378,000 of value and climbs through two middle tiers to 1.90% on value above $1,511,999.

A flat 1.90% applies to second homes, short-term rentals and vacant residential lots, and an empty inherited house usually lands there too. Leave a house empty during probate and its tax bill may climb above what the owner paid.

Under MCA 15-16-102, a late bill picks up a 2% penalty plus interest of 5/6 of 1% a month. Because the personal representative may pay taxes and assessments as an administration expense, there is no reason to let it slide.

Documents heirs need before listing

Expect the title company to ask who has authority to sign. This list is a typical start, and the title officer may add to it.

  • Certified death certificate.
  • Letters of appointment for the personal representative, or the recorded transfer on death deed.
  • A date-of-death appraisal to support the tax basis.
  • Current property tax bill and any delinquency notices.
  • A completed Realty Transfer Certificate, including the water right disclosure.

An inaccurate or incomplete certificate can bring a $500 penalty, six months in jail, or both, so even a family transfer needs care. Some transfers, such as a decedent's estate property or a termination of joint tenancy by death, are exceptions from providing sales price information.

When a cash sale makes sense for heirs

Heirs who live far away, dread repairs, or want the estate closed quickly sometimes prefer a cash sale. None of the tax rules above shift: the date-of-death basis, the property tax bill and the certificate filing are all the same.

The difference is speed and repair work. A house needing a roof, a cleanout or updating can go as-is at a price that reflects its condition. Weigh each offer against what it costs to carry the house through probate: taxes, insurance and utilities.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Does Montana have an inheritance tax?

No. The inheritance tax was repealed in November 2000 and does not apply to deaths after January 1, 2001.

Does Montana have an estate tax?

No. None applies to deaths after 2004. Very large estates can still face the federal tax, which has a $15,000,000 basic exclusion for deaths in 2026.

Do heirs pay tax when they inherit a house in Montana?

No Montana death tax is due. Income tax can follow if the house later sells for more than its date-of-death value, and the property tax bill passes to the heirs.

Who can sell an inherited house in Montana?

The personal representative, within the limits of the will and any court order, can sell estate real property at public or private sale under MCA 72-3-613. If title passed outside probate, the new owner sells instead.

Does the estate have to file a Montana income tax return?

Fiduciaries may need Form FID-3 if a federal Form 1041 was filed and the decedent owned Montana property or had Montana-source income.

What a Montana quitclaim deed does

A quitclaim deed hands over whatever interest the signer holds in a piece of real estate and makes no promise that the interest is any good. The sample form on the Montana courts site reads "does hereby convey, release, remise, and forever quit claim" to the grantee. It then names the county, describes the property, adds "together with the appurtenances," and ends with a notary block.

The wording matters. Under 70-20-304, MCA, using the word "grant" in a conveyance implies two covenants: the grantor has not already conveyed the same estate to someone else, and the estate carries no encumbrances the grantor created or allowed. A buyer can sue on those covenants as if they were written into the deed. The quitclaim form relies on "quit claim" language instead, so a buyer should not expect those assurances.

Put simply, the deed passes the signer's share and nothing more. An owner of the whole house passes the whole house. An owner of half passes half, and someone who owns nothing passes nothing.

Signing and recording requirements

To be recorded, the deed has to be signed, acknowledged before a notary, printed within a few format limits, and delivered with a Realty Transfer Certificate and the recording fee. The filing goes to the clerk and recorder of the county where the land sits.

Acknowledgment comes from 70-21-203, MCA: before recording, the signer must acknowledge the instrument, or a subscribing witness must prove it with notarized proof. Layout rules sit in 7-4-2636, MCA.

RequirementWhat Montana law requires
AcknowledgmentSigner acknowledges before a notary, or a subscribing witness proves execution (70-21-203)
Paper and inkBlue or black ink on white paper, 8 1/2 x 11 or 8 1/2 x 14 inches (7-4-2636)
Margins3 inches at the top of page one, 1 inch at the top of later pages, 1 inch at the bottom, 1/2 inch on the sides (7-4-2636)
Parties and propertyParty names on page one or two, plus a property description for a real property conveyance (7-4-2636)
Return addressName and mailing address of whoever gets the document back, upper left of page one (7-4-2636)
Transfer certificateRealty Transfer Certificate filed with the deed (15-7-305)

A notary's acknowledgment does not have to meet the color and margin rules, and an embossed seal is exempt from the margin rules. Everything else on the page should follow them.

What it costs to record

For a standard document the recording fee is $20 for page one and $10 for each added page or fraction of a page. A deed that misses the 7-4-2636 format standards pays the standard fee plus $10 more. Both amounts are set by 7-4-2637, MCA.

The fee schedule has a built-in change. Starting July 1, 2027, the Department of Revenue will set the fee by administrative rule and adjust it every two years using a consumer price index factor based on June 2025. A deed recorded after that date may cost more than the figures here, so get the current fee sheet from the clerk and recorder before you file.

Count the pages before you go. A short deed with a notary block often runs two pages, and a formatting slip costs more than fixing it ahead of time.

The Realty Transfer Certificate

Form RTC, the Realty Transfer Certificate, is a Department of Revenue form filed with the county clerk and recorder at the same time as the deed. Its job is to keep property records current and to collect sale price data for mass appraisal.

Seller (grantor) and buyer (grantee) names must be identical on the form and the deed. The form also asks for the last four digits of the Social Security or federal employer identification number of everyone in the transfer, and an Individual Taxpayer Identification number if a foreign national is involved.

Family transfers are where the exceptions come in. The certificate does not need to state the amount paid for any of these:

  • A gift, or a transfer in contemplation of death without consideration.
  • A transfer between spouses, or between parent and child, for nominal consideration.
  • A transfer to a revocable living trust.
  • Property of a decedent's estate, and the end of a joint tenancy or life estate by death.
  • A transfer under a court decree, except a sheriff's sale.
  • A correction or supplement to a recorded instrument that adds no consideration.

Transfer on death deeds work differently. Under Title 72, Chapter 6, Part 4, no certificate is needed when the deed is recorded. After the owner dies, the beneficiary files one with a copy of the recorded deed and a certified death certificate.

Why recording matters

Recording tells everyone else about the transfer. Under 70-21-302, MCA, a conveyance that is acknowledged or proved, certified and recorded as the law prescribes counts as constructive notice of its contents to later purchasers and mortgagees from the moment the county clerk receives it.

In practice, timing decides disputes. A signed deed left in a drawer gives the grantee no public protection. If the grantor later signs a second deed or a mortgage in favor of someone else, whoever recorded first stands in the stronger position. The statute also lets a certified copy of a recorded conveyance be recorded in another county with the same force as the original, which helps a family that owns land in more than one county.

Does a quitclaim trigger the due-on-sale clause?

It can. A due-on-sale clause allows a lender to demand the full loan balance when all or part of the property is transferred without written consent, and federal law generally lets lenders enforce it.

Section 341 of the Garn-St Germain Act, 12 U.S.C. 1701j-3, shields some transfers of residential property with fewer than five dwelling units. A lender may not call the loan because of:

  • A transfer to a relative that results from the borrower's death.
  • A transfer after which the borrower's spouse or children become an owner.
  • A transfer under a divorce decree, legal separation or property settlement that makes the spouse an owner.
  • A transfer into a living trust in which the borrower stays a beneficiary, if occupancy rights do not move.
  • A lease of three years or less with no purchase option.

A quitclaim to a friend, a business partner or an investor is outside that list. If the house has a mortgage, call the servicer before anyone signs.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Montana houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

When a quitclaim fits and when it does not

A quitclaim is the right tool when everyone already agrees who owns the house and the only goal is to change the name on title. It is the wrong tool when a buyer needs proof that title is clean.

  • Fits: adding or removing a spouse, moving the home into a revocable trust, a divorce settlement, a gift to a child, or releasing a co-owner's share.
  • Does not fit: a sale to an unrelated buyer who expects a title guarantee, a house with unknown heirs, or any property where liens may exist.

A quitclaim does not clear a lien. Montana Legal Services Association explains that unpaid property tax becomes a tax lien, and the county cannot release it until the tax, interest and penalties are paid. Deeding the house to a relative leaves the lien in place.

Tax class can shift with a new owner. For 2026, primary residences and long-term rentals are taxed on a tiered scale starting at 0.76%, while second homes, short-term rentals and vacant residential lots pay a flat 1.90%. A parent who deeds the family home to a child who will not live there may be moving it into the higher class.

Inherited, behind on payments, or in need of repairs

A quitclaim alone rarely fixes these situations.

  • Inherited with several heirs: every heir with an interest has to sign, and the estate paperwork must be in order before a buyer will close.
  • Behind on mortgage or taxes: the debt follows the property no matter whose name is on the deed.
  • Needs repairs: condition has no effect on how a deed works, but it does change what a buyer will pay.

If your real goal is to sell, a cash buyer can take the house as is, and the closing company prepares the deed, files the transfer certificate and handles recording. Call or text us, or ask for a written cash offer on the form at the top of this page. You are under no obligation to accept.

Frequently asked questions

Is a quitclaim deed legal in Montana?

Yes. Montana recognizes quitclaim deeds, and the courts publish a sample form. To be recorded, the deed must be acknowledged before a notary and filed with the county clerk and recorder along with a Realty Transfer Certificate and the recording fee.

How much does it cost to file a quitclaim deed in Montana?

The recording fee for a standard document is $20 for the first page and $10 for each added page, and $10 more if the format standards are not met. From July 1, 2027, the Department of Revenue will adjust the fee for inflation by rule.

Do I need a notary for a Montana quitclaim deed?

In practice, yes. Before recording, the signer must acknowledge the deed, or a subscribing witness must prove it with notarized proof (70-21-203, MCA).

Does a Montana quitclaim deed guarantee clear title?

No. Montana's implied covenants attach to the word "grant," and the quitclaim form uses "quit claim" language. The deed passes only what the signer owns and does not remove liens, unpaid taxes or other owners' interests.

Can a quitclaim deed make my lender call my mortgage?

It can, if the loan has a due-on-sale clause and the transfer is not protected. Federal law protects transfers to a relative after the borrower's death, to a spouse or children, in some divorces, and into a living trust where the borrower stays a beneficiary.

Does Montana tax capital gains when you sell a house?

Yes. Montana folds net long-term capital gains into its state income tax. Owning the house longer than a year and selling above your basis creates that kind of gain. The rates stay at 3.0% and 4.1% for tax years 2026 and 2027.

No separate real estate gains tax exists in Montana. Profit on the house is reported on Form 2, the Montana individual income tax return, together with your other income. A seller who qualifies for the federal home sale exclusion may owe little or nothing.

This page is general information. Confirm your own numbers with the Department of Revenue or a tax professional.

Montana capital gains rates and brackets

There are two capital gains rates, 3.0% and 4.1%, and which one applies depends on how your gain compares with your Montana ordinary income. The 2025 tables apply the lower rate to the first slice of gain, reduced by ordinary income, and 4.1% above it.

Where the 3.0% rate ends, tax year 2025
Filing status3.0% applies to first4.1% applies to
Single or married filing separately$21,100 of gain, minus ordinary incomeGain above that
Married filing jointly or surviving spouse$42,200 of gain, minus ordinary incomeGain above that
Head of household$31,700 of gain, minus ordinary incomeGain above that

If your ordinary income already exceeds the threshold, all of your net long-term gain is taxed at 4.1%. For 2026 and 2027, House Bill 337 keeps the 3.0% and 4.1% rates but adjusts the brackets to match its new ordinary income ranges.

The 2026 and 2027 income tax changes

House Bill 337 widens the lower ordinary income bracket and trims the upper rate, and it leaves the capital gains rates alone. Taxable income for these brackets does not include long-term capital gains, so the gain is taxed on its own schedule.

For 2026, the 4.7% rate applies up to $47,500 for a single filer, $71,250 for head of household and $95,000 for a married couple filing jointly, with an upper rate of 5.65%. For 2027, the 4.7% rate applies up to $65,000, $97,500 and $130,000 for those same statuses, and the upper rate drops to 5.4%. In 2025 the upper ordinary income rate was 5.9%. The bill also raises the Montana earned income tax credit to 20% of the federal credit starting in 2026.

The year of sale decides which set of brackets you use, so a December closing and a January closing can fall under different tables.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Montana house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Federal tax on the gain from selling your Montana home

Often there is none. Someone selling a primary residence can shield up to $250,000 of profit from federal tax, and a married couple filing together can shield up to $500,000. To qualify you need 24 months of ownership and 24 months of living in the house, both falling inside the five years that end on the sale date.

  • The ownership months and the living months need not overlap. Each just has to land somewhere in that five-year stretch.
  • If you already used the exclusion on a different home in the previous two years, you generally cannot use it again.
  • A Form 1099-S from the closing agent means the sale must be reported, even when every dollar of gain is excluded.
  • Schedule D and Form 8949 carry the report when they are required.
  • Members of the Uniformed Services, Foreign Service and intelligence community on qualified extended duty can pause the five-year clock for up to 10 years.

The IRS sale of your home topic and Publication 523 lay out the full rules. Profit beyond the exclusion is what flows to your Montana return at the rates above.

The Montana Realty Transfer Certificate

This form reports your sale to the state, which then compares it with income tax returns. It warns that you may owe income tax, since profit on the transfer counts as Montana-source income that belongs on a return.

Each seller lists the last four digits of a Social Security or federal ID number, and the department uses those digits to line certificates up with returns. A separate question asks whether the house was your principal residence, meaning you occupied it for at least seven months.

Hand it to the county clerk and recorder along with the deed at recording. Filing a false or missing form can mean a $500 penalty, six months in jail, or both.

Distressed sales get their own boxes: sheriff's deed, trustee's deed, deed in lieu of foreclosure and short sale. Another box covers transfers made as part of a 1031 or 1033 exchange.

Figuring your gain: basis, improvements and selling costs

Subtract your adjusted basis and your selling costs from the sale price and you have the gain. Basis begins at the purchase price and grows with capital improvements like a new roof or an added room. Ordinary upkeep and routine repairs leave it unchanged.

Hold on to these records:

  • The closing statement and price from your purchase.
  • Receipts for work that added value or extended the life of the house.
  • The settlement statement from this sale, showing commissions, title fees and credits to the buyer.

Selling as-is means you spend nothing on fix-up work, and it also means you add nothing to your basis before the sale. If your gain sits comfortably under the federal exclusion, that trade-off costs little in tax. If you are near the limit, talk to a tax adviser before choosing.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Montana houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling an inherited house after probate

An heir generally starts with a basis set at the house's fair market value on the day the owner died. Publication 551 covers this rule. The step-up wipes out most of the appreciation from the owner's lifetime, so an heir who lists the house soon after inheriting often reports a small gain or none at all. Gifted property follows different rules, so read Publication 551 for your case.

Get a date-of-death appraisal and file it with the estate papers. Without a Schedule A showing the estate tax value, the appraised value on that date is what you can use for state inheritance or transmission tax purposes. Our Montana estate and inheritance tax guide covers the estate side.

Moving to Montana or selling from another state

Montana's return gives a credit for income tax paid to another state or country on gains that Montana also taxes. Schedule III includes a line for that credit on Montana net long-term capital gains, set at the lesser of the figures on its worksheet lines.

If you do not live in Montana but sell Montana real estate, the gain is still Montana-source income, as the certificate states. A nonresident seller should expect Montana to want it reported, and a title or escrow officer can tell you what paperwork applies to your closing.

How a quick cash sale affects your taxes

A cash sale does not change the tax rules, only the timing and certainty. The same federal exclusion, Montana rates and reporting forms apply whether the buyer pays cash or uses a loan.

What you control is the paperwork. Selling costs reduce your gain, so ask for the settlement statement early and give it to your tax preparer.

Plan for the tax bill the following spring. Set aside part of your proceeds if you expect any gain above the exclusion, and keep the closing statement, the Realty Transfer Certificate copy and your basis records together.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

What is the Montana capital gains tax rate?

Montana taxes net long-term capital gains at 3.0% and 4.1%. Those rates stay in place for tax years 2026 and 2027, with brackets adjusted to match the new ordinary income ranges.

Does Montana have a separate tax on selling a house?

No. The gain is reported on your Montana individual income tax return, Form 2, and you file a Realty Transfer Certificate with the county clerk and recorder at recording.

How much of my home sale gain is excluded?

Federal law shields $250,000 of profit for one filer and $500,000 for joint filers, provided the house was your home for two of the last five years. Only profit above that is taxed, and a Form 1099-S still means you report the sale.

Is capital gains tax collected at closing in Montana?

No. You report the gain on your income tax return for the year of sale, so plan to set money aside. Unpaid property tax, by contrast, is paid from proceeds at closing.

What is the basis of a house I inherited in Montana?

Generally it is the fair market value on the date of death, as described in IRS Publication 551. Keep a date-of-death appraisal so you can support it. For tax questions, the Department of Revenue call center is (406) 444-6900.
